VeriCache: Turning Lossy KV Cache into Lossless LLM Inference

Jiayi Yao1, Samuel Shen2, Kuntai Du2, Shaoting Feng1, Dongjoo Seo3, Rui Zhang,
Yuyang Huang1, Yuhan Liu1, Shan Lu4,1, Junchen Jiang2,1 Affiliation: 1University of Chicago  2Tensormesh Inc.  3Samsung Semiconductor  4Microsoft Research email:
Received  5 June 2009
Abstract.

The large size of the KV cache has become a major bottleneck for serving LLMs with increasing context lengths. In response, many KV cache compression methods, such as token dropping and quantization, have been proposed. However, almost all of these methods are inherently lossy—despite minimal accuracy degradation for short outputs, their outputs increasingly diverge from full-KV-cache outputs as more tokens are decoded, which leads to catastrophic failures in code generation and tool calling.

We present VeriCache, the first inference framework that ensures the same output as full-KV-cache decoding but largely preserves the high decoding throughput of a range of KV cache compression algorithms. VeriCache uses the compressed KV cache to draft tokens, then verifies them against the full KV cache. While it may seem like just speculative decoding, VeriCache requires addressing a key system challenge to work—keeping the full KV cache out of GPU memory and minimizing the overhead of swapping it in for verification. The insight is two-fold: (1) compressed-KV decoding can be parallelized with full-KV swap, because one is HBM-bandwidth-bound and the other is PCIe/network-bound, and (2) the compressed KV cache often produces output similar to the full KV cache, allowing a long drafting horizon to amortize each full-KV swap.

VeriCache applies to both long-context decoding and remote prefix caching, supports a broad family of token-dropping and quantization methods through a uniform compressor interface, and composes with traditional speculative decoding. Experimental results show that VeriCache achieves up to 4×4\times higher throughput than full-KV inference while producing identical outputs.

1. Introduction

The context lengths of state-of-the-art LLMs have grown to more than one million tokens. This growth has powered many applications, from repository-level code generation (Gu et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2024; Seo et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2026), multi-document reasoning (Peper et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2025; Lei and Huang, 2025; Tan et al., 2025), to agentic workflows with long interaction histories (Steinberger, 2025; NVIDIA Corporation, 2026; OpenAI, 2026; Zhang et al., ).

The performance impact of KV cache manifests at both single-request and multi-request LLM serving. Within a single request, every decoding step must read the entire KV cache from GPU memory (HBM) to on-chip memory for attention. Furthermore, the size of the KV cache degrades request throughput, as it reduces the number of requests that can fit in GPU memory (Sun et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b). Across requests, KV cache reuse is a common practice to avoid repetitive KV cache generation among requests that share long common prefixes (e.g., system prompts, shared documents, prior conversation turns). Then large KV caches on storage need to be quickly loaded onto GPU memory when a request arrives, which can dominate request latency (Liu et al., 2024b; Liu et al., 2025b; Xiang et al., 2025).

A growing line of work tackles these problems by compressing the KV cache—either by dropping tokens at selected layers and attention heads (Xiao et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2026; Jegou and Jeblick, 2026; Devoto et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2024) or by reducing precision through quantization (Liu et al., 2024b; Hooper et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024c; Zandieh et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025a). Both deliver substantial efficiency gains—with 2–5×\times reductions in memory or transfer size.

Although effective at improving throughput, compressing KV cache changes its content , causing inference output to diverge from the distribution of decoding outputs using the full-size KV cache. As we will show in Section 3, the probability of divergence accumulates with more output tokens. When an application needs long output, the output divergence often violates functional correctness or structural requirements, even if the output is still smooth natural language. On coding and tool-calling benchmarks, functional accuracy (e.g., syntax validity, exact argument matching) degrades sharply even at moderate compression ratios.

This creates a dichotomy (Figure 1): accept lossy KV and risk output quality, or use full KV at the cost of much lower throughput. We pose the following question:

Can we exploit the throughput benefits of KV cache compression without affecting LLM output?

In this paper, we present VeriCache, a new inference scheme inspired by speculative decoding (Li et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2024b; Ouyang et al., 2024; Cai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a). Instead of directly serving tokens from compressed KV cache, VeriCache uses the compressed KV cache to draft tokens, then verifies them against the full KV cache. Wrong tokens are corrected, so the final output is identical 11 1 In this paper, we define identical results as identical under greedy decoding (i.e., zero temperature) except for randomness caused by hardware to full-KV inference.

Directly applying existing speculative decoding techniques is insufficient as token verification overhead can cause throughput degradation (see §4), negating the benefits of KV cache compression. VeriCache uses two key designs that take advantage of the fact that drafting and verification in VeriCache use exactly the same model and model weights, a property different from traditional speculative decoding.

First, VeriCache schedules cross-resource staggering. By sharing exactly the same model (weights), token drafting and token verification become feasible to execute in the same batch, offering a huge performance benefit as drafting and verification have complementary resource bottlenecks. Drafting decodes one token at a time using compressed KV located in GPU memory. Its sequential vector-matrix multiplication under-utilizes GPU FLOPs and makes it a GPU memory bandwidth bound operation. Verification, in contrast, requires loading the full KV cache from secondary storage into GPU and verifying multiple tokens in parallel, putting its bottleneck on inter-connect bandwidth and GPU FLOPs. Consequently, staggering drafting and verification across these distinct hardware resources offers much better utilization than running only drafting or only verification in each batch—the lock-step playbook in traditional speculative decoding. Cross-resource staggering requires much more sophisticated scheduling, which we will explain in §5.

Second, VeriCache uses an extended verification period that maximizes the parallelism of verification and minimizes the loading frequency of full KV cache. How often verification happens (i.e., every how many output tokens per verification) depends on how likely the drafted tokens would be accepted by the verification process. The more likely they are, the less frequent the verification can be. Different from traditional speculative decoding, compressed KV caches retain the same model weights and dominant attention patterns as the full model, so the compressed-KV drafter sustains much longer accepted runs than a traditional small-model drafter—25–40 accepted tokens per verification round for VeriCache vs. only 2–3 for typical small-model drafters (Section 4.3).

VeriCache handles both long-context decoding and remote prefix caching, with a runtime scheduler that adapts verification frequency and batch composition to hardware and workload conditions.

The idea of driving a speculative drafter from a sparser or compressed KV cache is not new. MagicDec (Sadhukhan et al., 2024) pairs a small-model drafter with a sparse KV cache; QuantSpec (Tiwari et al., 2025) and SparseSpec (Zhao et al., 2025) extend it to self-speculation with hierarchical quantization and dynamic sparse attention, respectively.

However, there are two key differences. First, prior systems all keep the full KV cache in GPU memory, capping compression’s throughput gains. In long-context decoding, they cannot realize compression’s batch-size or HBM-bandwidth benefits; VeriCache instead dedicates HBM to compressed KV and reloads the full KV from host DRAM only at verification (§4.2). In remote prefix caching—where the bottleneck is the slow storage-to-remote-GPU link, not HBM—no prior speculative-with-compressed-KV system applies; VeriCache’s remote drafter sees only the compressed KV over the slow link, while a local GPU on the fast link either caches or loads and applies the full KV for verification. In long-context decoding—the setting where prior systems apply—VeriCache also achieves higher throughput (§8).

Second, VeriCache enables lossless inference at a high throughput for a range of lossy KV cache compression techniques—quantization and token dropping—for the first time. VeriCache exposes a uniform compressor interface: any token-dropping or quantization method that conforms can serve as the drafter, with no change to scheduling, verification, or transfer (§6). We instantiate this interface for seven existing methods spanning token dropping and quantization, whereas prior systems hard-wire a single compressor.

VeriCache, built on top of vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) and LMCache (Liu et al., 2025b), achieves up to 4×4\times higher throughput than full-KV inference on long-context decoding and up to 2×2\times on remote prefix caching across models and workloads, with identical outputs.

2. Background

2.1. The KV cache bottleneck in inference

LLM inference consists of two phases: (1) prefill, which generates the KV cache for a prompt, and (2) decode, which generates tokens autoregressively from the KV cache. The KV cache introduces two overheads scaling with context length.

Within-request KV overhead. The KV cache incurs O⁡(n)O(n) memory footprint and bandwidth cost that grows linearly with context length nn (Xu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025a; Haoyang et al., 2025). On the memory side, larger KV caches leave less room for batching requests: serving Qwen-32B (Team, 2025) (∼{\sim}64GB weights) on a single H100 80GB GPU, a 2K-token context requires ∼{\sim}0.3GB of KV per request, allowing a batch of ∼{\sim}50 requests; scaling to 100K tokens grows the KV to ∼{\sim}15GB, reducing the batch size to 1. On the bandwidth side, each decode step must read the full KV from HBM: serving Llama-3.1-8B-1M (Xu et al., 2025b) (∼{\sim}16GB weights) on an H100 (3TB/s HBM), each decode step takes ∼{\sim}5ms at 5K context (∼{\sim}0.6GB KV) and ∼{\sim}25ms at 500K context (∼{\sim}60GB KV)—decoding 100 tokens takes ∼{\sim}0.5s at 5K context but ∼{\sim}2.5s at 500K.

Cross-request KV overhead. Many long-context workloads share long prefixes across requests—system prompts, shared documents, prior conversation turns—making the O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}) prefill redundantly expensive when each request recomputes them from scratch. To avoid this, systems precompute KV caches once and reuse them across requests (Liu et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2024). However, reusing a precomputed cache requires transferring KV caches from storage or across the network onto the serving GPU, and this transfer can itself become the new bottleneck at long contexts (Chen et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2024b; Xiang et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2024). For example, loading Qwen-32B’s precomputed KV cache from S3 (∼{\sim}3GB/s (Amazon Web Services, 2025)) takes ∼{\sim}0.5s at 10K context (∼{\sim}1.5GB) but ∼{\sim}5s at 100K context (∼{\sim}15GB)—matching or exceeding the prefill time reuse was meant to avoid.

2.2. KV cache compression techniques

A growing line of work tackles these bottlenecks by compressing the KV cache (Table 1). These methods fall into two categories. Token dropping changes the shape of the cache by dropping tokens at certain layers and attention heads. For example, StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) retains only a few initial “attention sink” tokens plus a sliding window of recent tokens, enabling unbounded generation. DuoAttention (Xiao et al., 2024) identifies attention heads that need full context and drops most entries for the rest. KVzip (Kim et al., 2025) scores KV pair importance via a context reconstruction loss at prefill and evicts low-importance pairs once for reuse across queries. FastKVzip (Kim et al., 2026) learns a per-token gating function that evicts low-importance entries. KV quantization preserves the cache shape but reduces its per-element precision—for example, KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024) quantizes keys per-channel before rotary positional embedding to preserve outlier structure at sub-4-bit precision. KIVI (Liu et al., 2024c) applies per-channel quantization to keys and per-token to values for tuning-free 2-bit compression. TurboQuant (Zandieh et al., 2025) randomly rotates key/value vectors to induce a known coordinate distribution, enabling optimal per-coordinate scalar quantization at 2–4 bits without calibration. CacheGen (Liu et al., 2024b) encodes KV tensors into compact bitstreams by exploiting token-wise locality and layer-wise sensitivity.

Inherently lossy. All these compression methods are inherently lossy: the compressed KV cache deviates from the original, and these deviations propagate through inference.

3. Motivation: Why Lossy KV Methods Fail

3.1. Semantic similarity ≠\neq functional correctness

Previous KV compression techniques have been evaluated using token-level metrics (Adnan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024c; Yang et al., 2025; Zandieh et al., 2025), such as F1, ROUGE, perplexity, and cosine similarity. These token-level metrics tolerate small text deviation and are suitable for open-ended or short-answer tasks such as summarization, natural language Q&A, etc. However, they are ill-fitted for applications that have strict syntax or semantics requirement. For example, an invalid syntax token can break a program; a misplaced delimiter can corrupt a JSON object; and a wrong operator alters the semantics of a shell command (e.g., rm -rf *.logs →\to rm -rf * .). Figure 2 shows a real code-generation failure caused by the use of compressed KV.

Figure 3 illustrates this significant difference between a token-level metric (F1) and functional metrics (i.e., code format accuracy and function call accuracy). These two types of metrics are measured when we apply a representative token-dropping method, KVzip (Kim et al., 2025), on Qwen3-Coder-30B (Team, 2025). The left figure shows the results on a coding task in SWE-bench Lite (Jimenez et al., 2024); the right figure shows the results on a tool-calling task in ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025).

The pattern is consistent across both tasks: F1, which gives partial credit for partially correct outputs, remains above 75%, but functional correctness collapses (Liu et al., 2023a). Code format accuracy—which requires the output to be a syntactically valid git diff—drops to near zero under KVzip 4×\times compaction. Function call accuracy—which requires every call name and argument to match exactly—drops below 10% under KVzip 4×\times compaction.

For some of the fastest-growing LLM use cases including code generation, agentic tool use, and any tasks that require structured output, traditional token-level metrics are too lenient: any partial token-level deviation could be devastating.

3.2. Root cause: per-token bias accumulation

The quality collapse shown in Figure 3 reflects a fundamental limitation of KV compression. The altered KV cache changes the attention weights at every layer. It replaces the model’s learned next-token distribution pfullp_{\text{full}} with a different distribution plossyp_{\text{lossy}} that the model was never trained to produce. Unlike sampling noise (e.g., temperature), which draws different tokens within pfullp_{\text{full}}, this is a systematic bias: every sample is drawn from the wrong distribution, and no amount of resampling corrects it.

Per-step distribution shift.

We quantify this bias with the KL divergence (Reza, 1994) between the full-KV and lossy-KV next-token distributions at each decoding step tt:

(1) KLt=∑xtpfull​(xt∣x<t)​log⁡pfull​(xt∣x<t)plossy​(xt∣x<t).\mathrm{KL}_{t}\;=\;\sum_{x_{t}}p_{\text{full}}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})\,\log\frac{p_{\text{full}}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})}{p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})}.

KLt\mathrm{KL}_{t} is zero only when the two conditional distributions are identical, and grows as they diverge.

Distribution shift compounds over the generation.

This per-step bias accumulates over the autoregressive generation. By the chain rule of KL divergence:

(2) KL1:T≜KL(pfull(x1:T)∥plossy(x1:T))=∑t=1T𝔼x<t∼pfull[KLt].\mathrm{KL}_{1:T}\;\triangleq\;\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\text{full}}(x_{1:T})\,\|\,p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{1:T})\right)\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{x_{<t}\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\left[\mathrm{KL}_{t}\right].

if per-step KL exceeds ε>0\varepsilon>0, sequence-level KL grows linearly: KL1:T≥εT\mathrm{KL}_{1:T}\geq\varepsilon T. Since KL1:T\mathrm{KL}_{1:T} equals 𝔼x∼pfull[log(pfull(x1:T)/plossy(x1:T))]\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\big[\log(p_{\text{full}}(x_{1:T})/p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{1:T}))\big], this means that for a sequence sampled from pfullp_{\text{full}}, the log-likelihood ratio has mean ≥ε​T{\geq}\,\varepsilon T, and so the likelihood ratio pfull(x1:T)/plossy(x1:T)p_{\text{full}}(x_{1:T})/p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{1:T}) is typically of order eε​Te^{\varepsilon T}—i.e., exponential in TT (proof in Appendix A). Figure 4 confirms this empirically: KL1:T\mathrm{KL}_{1:T} grows linearly with decoding steps under both KVzip 4×\times compaction and TurboQuant k4v3 quantization.

Concretely, in Figure 4, KVzip 4×\times accumulates only ∼0.023{\sim}0.023 nats of KL per step—so the lossy model assigns the full-KV token e−0.023≈98%e^{-0.023}{\approx}98\% of its full-KV probability, barely distinguishable. After T=250T{=}250 steps, cumulative KL reaches ∼6{\sim}6 nats, so the lossy model emits the full-KV output sequence with probability only e−6≈2.5×10−3e^{-6}{\approx}2.5{\times}10^{-3}—the ∼2%{\sim}2\% per-step gap amplified into a 400×400\times mismatch over a few hundred tokens. Figure 2 shows the consequence: on a long code generation task, the 4×\times compacted output starts correctly but rapidly degenerates as compounding bias drives the model off its learned distribution.

The accuracy-efficiency dichotomy.

For precision-critical applications, existing KV compressions force a binary choice: accept lossy KV and risk silent failures, or use full KV and forgo the efficiency gains. We argue that this dichotomy is unnecessary: compression should not replace exact computation, but accelerate it without sacrificing correctness.

4. KV Cache Verification

4.1. VeriCache overview

At the algorithm level, VeriCache repurposes any lossy KV compression method into a speculative execution layer of the inference pipeline, where tokens are drafted quickly. These drafted tokens are then verified against the full KV cache to guarantee correctness (Figure 5). Concretely, let KVcomp\text{KV}_{\text{comp}} denote the compressed KV cache and KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{full}} the full cache. The core loop proceeds as follows22 2 We describe greedy decoding for clarity; VeriCache extends to sampling-based decoding via standard rejection sampling (Li et al., 2025c; Ouyang et al., 2024).:

(1) Draft: autoregressively generate xx candidate tokens t1,…,txt_{1},\dots,t_{x} using KVcomp\text{KV}_{\text{comp}}—each tit_{i} is the most-likely next token under the model’s distribution conditioned on the prompt (represented by KVcomp\text{KV}_{\text{comp}}) and the previously generated tokens.

(2) Verify: one forward pass over the xx drafted positions in parallel, conditioned on KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{full}} and t1..k−1t_{1..k-1} at each position kk. A single forward pass yields x+1x{+}1 predictions t1∗,…,tx+1∗t_{1}^{*},\dots,t_{x+1}^{*}: one at each drafted position kk (the full-KV next-token prediction given t1..k−1t_{1..k-1}), plus one bonus prediction tx+1∗t_{x+1}^{*} that follows the last drafted token.

(3) Accept: find the first position j∈[1,x]j\in[1,x] where tj≠tj∗t_{j}\neq t_{j}^{*}; accept t1,…,tj−1t_{1},\dots,t_{j-1} and the verifier’s correction tj∗t_{j}^{*}, and discard the rest. If all xx drafted tokens match (no such jj exists), accept all xx of them plus the bonus tx+1∗t_{x+1}^{*}. Drafting then resumes from the position immediately after the last accepted token.

At the system level, each verify step demands three resources beyond drafting: (1) interconnect bandwidth to load KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{full}} from CPU or remote storage, (2) GPU HBM to hold it during the verify pass (competing with resident compressed caches), and (3) GPU compute for the verify pass over xx tokens. The first two are tightly budgeted and lock-step verification would spike both; compute is handled implicitly, since staggering verifies across iterations (§5) smooths the compute. Without care, these costs would erase compression’s throughput gain. We next present two design principles (P1, P2) that let VeriCache pay for verification without giving it back. The runtime mechanisms that realize these principles are detailed in Section 5.

4.2. P1: Cross-resource staggering

Traditional speculative decoding runs requests in lock-step: all draft for xx iterations, then all verify at iteration x+1x{+}1. Every iteration shares the same bottleneck, leaving other resources idle.

VeriCache’s first design principle is to stagger requests instead, mixing some requests’ verification into iterations where others are drafting. Since compressed-KV drafting and full-KV verification consume complementary resources (elaborated below), staggering yields much better resource utilization. We describe the design for both use cases below; the runtime mechanics appear in §5.

4.2.1. Staggering with long-context decoding

Deployment and resource consumption

Traditionally, when compressed KV is used for long-context decoding, the KV cache is kept in compressed form in GPU high-performance memory (HBM) throughout serving, and the full KV is never retained on the GPU. In subsequent iterations, the compressed KV cache is read from HBM to help generate the next token(s).

In VeriCache, we keep all the traditional setting and in addition, keep the full in CPU memory as shown in Figure 7. Whenever this request’s drafted tokens are ready to be verified, the full KV is reloaded from CPU to GPU over the CPU–GPU interconnect, and used for verification.

Under this setting, the performance of drafting is bounded by HBM-bandwidth: the GPU spends an iteration to read model weights and the compressed KV cache from HBM, with little compute (i.e., forward pass for one token) to do. In contrast, the performance of verification draws on different resources entirely: it must transfer KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{full}} across an interconnect (CPU–GPU) and run a forward pass over xx drafted tokens, putting its bottleneck on interconnect bandwidth and GPU compute rather than HBM bandwidth.

Staggering schedule & performance estimation

We now discuss our staggering schedule in more details, together with a performance estimation; the full derivations with relaxed assumptions are in Appendix B. Table 2 summarizes the notation.

Consider a single GPU serving BB long-context requests. Each request keeps KVcomp=c⋅KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{comp}}=c\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}} on GPU and KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{full}} on CPU. Cross-resource staggering schedules verifications so that, at any iteration, only about B/xB/x of the BB requests are in the verify phase, each checking the xx tokens it most recently drafted. Per iteration, the GPU does BB single-token forward passes for the drafting requests plus ∼(B/x)⋅x=B{\sim}(B/x)\cdot x=B token forward passes for the staggered verifications—roughly 2​B2B tokens total. The HBM traffic these passes incur has three components: the model weights (MM), the compressed KV cache of every drafting request (B⋅c⋅KVfullB\cdot c\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}, the compressed-KV bandwidth used by drafting), and the full KV cache of the B/xB/x verifying requests ((B/x)⋅KVfull(B/x)\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}, the full-KV bandwidth used by verification). In parallel, the next B/xB/x full KV caches transfer from CPU to GPU over the interconnect, overlapping with the forward passes. The iteration time TiterT_{\text{iter}} is therefore the longer of the GPU forward-pass time TgpuT_{\text{gpu}} and the CPU–GPU transfer time TxferT_{\text{xfer}}:

(3) Titer=max⁡(M+B⋅KVfull⋅(c+1/x)BWhbm⏟Tgpu,B⋅KVfullx⋅BWinter⏟Txfer)T_{\text{iter}}=\max\!\Big(\underbrace{\frac{M+B\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}\cdot(c+1/x)}{\text{BW}_{\text{hbm}}}}_{T_{\text{gpu}}},\;\;\underbrace{\frac{B\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}}{x\cdot\text{BW}_{\text{inter}}}}_{T_{\text{xfer}}}\Big)

This staggered schedule offers better resource utilization than the traditional lock-step schedule that conducts all-draft iterations followed by all-verify iterations: the all-draft iterations leave the CPU-GPU link idle; even if CPU-GPU transfer overlaps with drafting iterations, the resource utilization of all-verify iterations would still be a concern. Assume that requests B1B_{1}, B2B_{2} … BkB_{k} are scheduled to enter the same all-verify iteration. Transferring their full KVs from CPU to GPU will take a lot of time, much longer than one forward-pass iteration. Even worse, since the transfer is serial, the full KV of B1B_{1} will have to stay in the HBM idle, waiting for the full KVs of B2B_{2}, … BkB_{k} to arrive before the verification starts. We further explain this comparison with a concrete example below.

Concrete example. Consider serving Mistral 24B on an RTX PRO 6000 (PCIe Gen5 ×16\times 16, 64 GB/s) with B=10B{=}10 requests, KVcomp=1\text{KV}_{\text{comp}}{=}1 GB and KVfull=4\text{KV}_{\text{full}}{=}4 GB per request, and draft length x=30x{=}30. Each verify transfers one KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{full}} over PCIe (∼80\sim 80 ms). A draft-only iteration reads M+B⋅KVcompM+B\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{comp}} from HBM (∼35\sim 35 ms); folding in a verify adds one KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{full}} to the HBM read, extending it to ∼37\sim 37 ms. With VeriCache, the 1010 verifies are spread one every 33 draft iterations, so each ∼80\sim 80-ms PCIe transfer overlaps with concurrent draft work and peak HBM stays at M+B⋅KVcomp+1⋅KVfull=64M+B\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{comp}}+1\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}=64 GB. A lock-step alternative that batches all 1010 verifies at iteration 3030 serializes 4040 GB on the single PCIe link (∼800\sim 800 ms of transfer time, ∼20×\sim 20\times the iteration window) and spikes HBM to M+B⋅KVfull=90M+B\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}=90 GB (assuming compressed cache is offloaded to CPU). A sequential variant (one verify per iteration after drafting) avoids the HBM spike but still pays the same ∼800\sim 800 ms of PCIe transfer overhead per 3030-token draft cycle that staggering eliminates.

4.2.2. Staggering with remote prefix caching

Deployment and resource consumption

Traditionally, in remote prefix caching, pre-computed KV caches are saved on a storage node. When an incoming request’s prefix matches one, the KV is transferred to a remote serving GPU before decoding can begin. Because the serving GPUs connect to the storage node over a slow link, transferring the compressed KV greatly reduces this transfer time.

VeriCache additionally leverages the storage node’s local GPU for verification (Figure 7): on a prefix match, the storage node sends the compressed KV through the slow link to the remote GPU for drafting, and the full KV through the fast link to its local GPU for verification. Drafting and verification thus run on completely different hardware.

Staggering schedule & performance estimation

Drafting (remote, HBM-bound) and verifying (local, storage-bandwidth-bound load plus a forward pass) use distinct hardware, so VeriCache pipelines them within a single request as follows. Every xx drafted tokens trigger one verify: the remote drafter advances xx tokens on the compressed KV cache while, in parallel, the local verifier prefetches the full KV cache from storage over BWh\text{BW}_{h}. When both finish, the local runs a forward pass over those xx positions; the remote then waits for the accept/reject result before drafting the next xx tokens. So per-request, only the verify transfer hides behind drafting—the verify forward pass itself sits on the critical path, because the next xx drafts depend on which of the previous xx were accepted. At the system level, while the remote pool waits on request rr’s verify forward pass, it drafts for other requests in the batch, so no GPU is ever idle. The per-request time is:

(4) Treq=c⋅KVfullBWl⏟startup+Kx​γ​(x,c)⏟# draft-verify cycles⋅TcycleT_{\text{req}}=\underbrace{\frac{c\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}}{\text{BW}_{l}}}_{\text{startup}}+\underbrace{\frac{K}{x\,\gamma(x,c)}}_{\text{\# draft-verify cycles}}\cdot T_{\text{cycle}}

where Tcycle=max⁡(x⋅Tdecode,KVfull/BWh)+Tfwd​(x)T_{\text{cycle}}=\max\!\big(x\cdot T_{\text{decode}},\;\text{KV}_{\text{full}}/\text{BW}_{h}\big)+T_{\text{fwd}}(x): the max\max captures the draft–load overlap, and Tfwd​(x)T_{\text{fwd}}(x) is paid serially after it. The startup is ∼1/c×{\sim}1/c\times faster than the full-KV baseline (KVfull/BWl\text{KV}_{\text{full}}/\text{BW}_{l}), and γ⁡(x,c)\gamma(x,c) directly reduces the number of draft-verify cycles needed.

4.3. P2: High acceptance rate amortizes verification

Observation 2: xx and γ\gamma together govern verification cost.

Given a compression ratio cc, the draft length xx sets how often verification fires (once per x+1x{+}1 iterations) and the acceptance rate γ⁡(x,c)\gamma(x,c) sets how many drafted tokens each round actually keeps. If xx is too small, verification fires too often and the verification overhead dominates; if γ\gamma is too low, most drafted tokens are discarded and the work in each round is wasted. Verification amortizes cheaply only when both xx and γ\gamma are high.

Insight 1.

Because VeriCache’s drafter is the target model itself running on the compressed KV cache, the compressed cache preserves the model’s weights and the dominant attention patterns. The drafted tokens therefore closely track the full-KV output, so γ\gamma stays high even at long draft lengths—verification fires rarely and a large fraction of each round’s drafted tokens are accepted.

Figure 8 confirms this on 20 samples from the LMCache agentic trace (LMCache, 2025), running Llama-70B on 2×\timesH100 NVL under KVzip (Kim et al., 2025) compaction. The left panel shows that at 4×4\times compaction, the acceptance rate stays above ∼0.8{\sim}0.8 even at draft length 3030---each verification round keeps a large fraction of its drafted tokens. The right panel translates this into ideal speedup33 3 Computed using the detailed throughput model in Appendix B, which accounts for pipelined reloads and GPU memory constraints; Eq. (11) is a simplified version capturing the same tradeoffs.: VeriCache reaches a peak of ∼3.7×{\sim}3.7\times at draft length 1515. The dashed curve includes the verification overhead (after request staggering) and lies slightly below the solid (no-overhead) upper bound, with the residual gap—visible mostly at short draft lengths.

By comparison, traditional speculative decoding drafts tokens from a small auxiliary model whose parameters differ from the target; because the two distributions diverge quickly, typical small-model drafters sustain only a few accepted tokens (Provatas et al., 2026; Agrawal et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a). VeriCache keeps the target model and merely swaps in compressed KV, which is why its acceptance length stretches an order of magnitude further. Figure 9 quantifies the gap on Qwen-32B and Llama-70B: at draft length 3030, VeriCache at 4×4\times compaction sustains acceptance lengths of ∼19{\sim}19 on Qwen-32B and ∼23{\sim}23 on Llama-70B, while Eagle saturates near 11–22 on both, and a small draft model reaches only ∼3{\sim}3 on Qwen-32B and ∼10{\sim}10 on Llama-70B.

The two drafting strategies compose naturally: a small-model drafter (e.g., MTP (Cai et al., 2025), EAGLE (Li et al., 2025c)) proposes tokens that VeriCache verifies against the compressed KV, periodically rechecking against the full KV to correct compression errors. Figure 10 shows the payoff: VeriCache + Eagle reaches 4.35×4.35\times ideal speedup vs. 3.50×3.50\times for VeriCache alone and 1.78×1.78\times for Eagle alone (Appendix C).

5. VeriCache Runtime

The VeriCache runtime realizes the cross-resource staggering of §4: it decides which requests draft or verify at each iteration and schedules KV transfers so each verify lands on time. It maintains a resource model of the interconnect and GPU HBM, then places each request’s next verify in a window with spare capacity—a placement made flexible by the high acceptance rate (§4.3).

5.1. Resource model

The runtime maintains WW future iterations horizon, indexed i∈[0,W)i\in[0,W), tracking two reserve rings across the windows:

BW ring (interconnect).

T⁡[i]T[i] holds the interconnect time already reserved for transfers landing in window ii. The link is serialized—one transfer at a time, with a transfer’s duration on the link equal to its size divided by the link’s bandwidth BW—so the constraint is

T⁡[i]≤Titer∀i∈[0,W).T[i]\leq T_{\text{iter}}\quad\forall i\in[0,W).

Both KV loads at request arrival (compressed for speculating requests, full for non-speculating) and verify reloads on each speculative round share this ring. For request rr with KVfull(r)\text{KV}_{\text{full}}^{(r)}, the reload’s iteration-equivalent duration is ℓr=KVfull(r)/(BW⋅Titer)\ell_{r}=\text{KV}_{\text{full}}^{(r)}/(\text{BW}\cdot T_{\text{iter}}), spanning Sr=max⁡(1,⌈ℓr⌉)S_{r}=\max(1,\,\lceil\ell_{r}\rceil) windows.

HBM ring (GPU memory).

B⁡[i]B[i] holds the in-flight KV cache occupying HBM during window ii—KV streaming onto the GPU for an upcoming verify but not yet consumed by it. Together with persistent residency, the constraint is

M+KVresident+B⁡[i]≤HBM∀i∈[0,W),M+\text{KV}_{\text{resident}}+B[i]\leq\text{HBM}\quad\forall i\in[0,W),

where MM is the model weights and KVresident\text{KV}_{\text{resident}} counts every KV cache kept on the GPU between iterations—compressed for drafting requests, full for pinned or non-speculating ones.

GPU compute is not modeled as a third ring: VeriCache’s cross-resource staggering (§4.2) spreads verifies evenly across iterations, so compute load is smoothed rather than bursting.

5.2. Request admission and execution loop

Request admission.

VeriCache runtime conducts an Admit operation (See Algorithm 1) at request arrival and again after every verify. It either picks a future verify iteration drd_{r} within its lookahead window—reserving the full-KV-cache transfer that must complete by drd_{r}—or returns rr to waiting queue.

The search for the next verify iteration starts from checking whether the xx-th iteration from now is feasible — xx is the draft length that maximizes ideal speedup (Figure 8 in §4.3), typically 2020–5050. VeriCache runtime looks at its resource model to see if there is sufficient interconnect to reload the full KV back to GPU likely before the iteration xx and whether there is sufficient HBM resource to hold the full KV. When xx does not work, the runtime checks the x−1x-1th and the x+1x+1th iteration from now, then x−2x-2 and x+2x+2, and so on; each candidate window indexes both rings simultaneously, and a reservation spans SrS_{r} consecutive windows on both. The first candidate that satisfies the BW-ring and HBM-ring constraints (§5.1) is reserved; if none does, rr is returned to waiting queue.

Execution loop.

At each iteration tt, the runtime performs three steps: (i) Kick off verify reloads. For each speculating request whose reserved span has its first window at iteration tt, start the asynchronous full-KV-cache reload on the link feeding the verifying GPU. (ii) Draft and verify. Draft run the next iteration’s forward pass; concurrently, the verify completes the verify forward pass for each request whose scheduled iteration is the current one. For each completed verify, re-invoke Admit(r)(r) with the updated state—either continuing speculation with the next verify iteration scheduled, or returning rr to the waiting queue. (iii) Advance. Slide the lookahead window one iteration forward.

5.3. Per-setting specialization

The two settings differ in their interconnects and in whether the verifying GPU is the same physical device as the drafter.

Long-context decoding.

Drafting and verification share the serving GPU, and the interconnect is the CPU↔\leftrightarrowGPU link. The BW ring (§5.1) tracks reservations on this link, and the HBM ring tracks the same GPU’s HBM usage. The compressed cache stays on GPU for drafting, and each verify reloads the full KV cache from CPU.

Remote prefix caching.

Two GPU pools share a storage node (Figure 7): a small local pool on a fast link BWh\text{BW}_{h}, and a larger remote pool on a slow link BWl≪BWh\text{BW}_{l}\ll\text{BW}_{h}. Remote-pool requests speculate: the remote GPU drafts using the compressed KV cache streamed over BWl\text{BW}_{l}, while a local GPU concurrently loads the full KV cache over BWh\text{BW}_{h} for an upcoming verify and runs the verify forward pass for a request whose KV has already arrived. Because VeriCache issues each load ahead of its verify deadline, drafting, loading, and verifying all pipeline together. All links and pool HBMs are tracked by their own BW/HBM rings (§5.1): BWl\text{BW}_{l} carries initial compressed-KV loads to remote drafters, BWh\text{BW}_{h} carries verify reloads, and each pool’s HBM ring tracks HBM usage.

6. Compressor Interface

KV cache compression methods differ in what they produce: some drop token positions per (layer, head), others quantize entries to lower precision. VeriCache’s runtime relies on a small interface (Listing 1) that exposes only what it needs to allocate HBM and run attention—which positions are dropped, and bits per element.

Offline means the compression step runs off the serving GPU (on CPU or an idle GPU), since methods often need information not computed by normal inference (e.g., explicit attention weights) or extra forward passes that would slow inline serving. Online compression runs inline through update, with decisions driven by per-iteration state.

The interface is pass-through: the runtime hands the compressor the physical-layout metadata and lets it gather, dequantize, or write pages itself. update mirrors this by passing req_offsets for batch slicing. The cost—compressor authors must understand the runtime’s paged layout—avoids a virtualization layer; KIVI’s fused dequant-attention already operates on pages directly.

Long-context decoding.

The runtime keeps the compressed cache in HBM and drafts against it. With offline compression, for example, KVzip (Kim et al., 2025) scores tokens by context reconstructability and keeps, say, 25% per (layer, head) of a 100K-token context; compress runs offline and returns CompressedKV with the 75K evicted positions per (layer, head) and bit_scheme=16, after which the runtime allocates pages for the retained 25K and runs sparse attention with decompress never called. With online compression, for example, KVzap (Jegou and Jeblick, 2026) scores tokens during inference with a small MLP on hidden state: compress initializes dropped_indices to empty; after each layer’s forward, the runtime calls update(layer,q,k,v,hidden,req_offsets) on the batched tensors, and the compressor slices the batch via req_offsets, scores per request, and returns a (num_heads, new_drops) tensor per request. The runtime appends the new drops to dropped_indices[layer] and trims the (layer, head) page allocation.

Remote prefix caching.

The runtime never inspects the compressed cache: compress produces a payload at storage, the runtime streams the bytes, and decompress(compressed) materializes full KV at the remote drafter. The payload is a blob the compressor can fill however it wants.

Scope.

The interface targets deployment-time substitution under four constraints: (i) heads within a layer may drop different positions but the same number of tokens (count varies only across layers); (ii) the system runs one mode at a time; token-dropping and quantization do not mix across concurrent requests; (iii) bit_scheme is uniform across tokens and layers; (iv) the compression method is fixed at deployment. Each is a straightforward future-work extension. We instantiate the interface for seven methods.

7. Implementation

VeriCache is a thin layer between the request frontend and the GPU workers, built atop vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) (serving engine) and LMCache (Liu et al., 2025b) (persistent KV cache storage and transfer). VeriCache is implemented with  8K LoC of Python and C++.

VeriCache subclasses vLLM’s AsyncScheduler and manages its own GPU KV allocations so that compressed and transient reload KVs can coexist under our admission control. A scheduler hook runs Admit (Algorithm 1) against the BW and HBM rings of §5.1 and kicks each request’s verify reload asynchronously SrS_{r} windows ahead of its deadline; the bytes themselves move via LMCache, which exposes lookup/lookup_compressed returning (compressed) KV pointers, move for cross-tier transfers (CPU↔\leftrightarrowGPU, storage↔\leftrightarrowGPU), and a wrapper that invokes the Compressor of §6 on a stored KV pointer. Per-layer attention activations are routed through a forward hook to Compressor.update for online compressors; offline compressors run before serving (or on idle compute) and apply when the context’s KV is reused.

8. Results

8.1. Evaluation settings

Models and hardware.

Mistral-24B (Mistral AI, 2025) and Qwen-32B (Team, 2025) run on a NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB); Llama-70B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) runs on 2×\timesH100 NVL (94 GB, TP==2). Each node connects CPU–GPU via PCIe 5.0 x16 (64 GB/s); the local node reaches the KV store at 4040 GB/s, remote nodes at 1.21.2 GB/s.

Two evaluation pipelines.

Pipeline 1 (long-context decoding) precomputes the context’s KV in CPU memory or storage and compresses it offline or online (§6); a single serving instance. Pipeline 2 (remote prefix caching) reuses KV across requests over the slow remote link with one local and four remote instances.

Compression methods.

Token dropping: KVzip (Kim et al., 2025), KVZap (Jegou and Jeblick, 2026), ExpectedAttention (Devoto et al., 2025), SnapKV (Li et al., 2024a). Quantization: KIVI (Liu et al., 2024c), KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024), RotateKV (Su et al., 2025).

Speculative-decoding baselines.

Traditional: EAGLE3 (Li et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2024b) auxiliary drafter, with RedHatAI pretrained speculators for Llama-70B (RedHat AI, 2025a) and Qwen-32B (RedHat AI, 2025b). Self-speculative: SparseSpec (Zhao et al., 2025), which drafts on the target model with PillarAttn (sparse attention selecting critical tokens via prior-verification scores) and verifies with full attention over resident full KV.

Datasets and quality metrics.

We use five datasets, each with its own quality metric:

  • •

    LMCache-trace (LMCache, 2025): both pipelines, offline+online (900 samples); KL-divergence from Full KV.

  • •

    ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025): Pipeline 1 offline (150 samples); fraction of function calls with exactly-matching arguments.

  • •

    PISanitizer (Geng et al., 2025): Pipeline 1 offline (50 samples); defense success rate against prompt injection.

  • •

    LongGenBench (Wu et al., 2024): Pipeline 1 online (50 samples); fraction of per-prompt constraints satisfied (completion rate).

  • •

    GSM8K-Long (Liu et al., 2024a): Pipeline 1 online (100 samples); fraction of chained math problems answered exactly.

Efficiency metrics.

End-to-end request latency (s) and throughput (tok/s).

8.2. Comparing with full KV and traditional speculative decoding

Throughout this comparison, VeriCache uses KVzip (compression ratio 0.20.2, anchored draft length x=25x{=}25) as its compressed-KV drafter on Pipeline 1 and KIVI (4-bit, x=40x{=}40) on Pipeline 2.

Figure 11 compares VeriCache against Full KV, a traditional drafter, SparseSpec, and VeriCache + traditional drafter on three models. On long-context decoding, VeriCache delivers 1.92×1.92\times–2.73×2.73\times over Full KV (e.g., 256256 vs. 102102 tok/s on Llama-70B), beating the traditional drafter, whose speedup is bounded by the unchanged KV footprint. Composing VeriCache with the drafter peaks at 4.26×4.26\times (Qwen-32B), as the two attack orthogonal bottlenecks: VeriCache shrinks per-request KV to enable larger batches, the drafter speeds up tokens within each request. On remote prefix caching, drafter-based methods do not apply; VeriCache still gives 1.33×1.33\times–2.11×2.11\times over Full KV (e.g., 485485 vs. 240240 tok/s on Llama-70B).

Varying hardware (Pipeline 1).

Figure 13 sweeps the two hardware axes that dominate long-context decoding. Left: the KV-cache budget, varied by serving Qwen-8B, Qwen-14B, Mistral-24B, and Qwen-32B (larger weights leave less HBM for KV). As the budget shrinks from 0.740.74 to 0.20.2 of HBM, VeriCache’s speedup grows from 1.61×1.61\times to 2.71×2.71\times—Full KV’s batch collapses faster than VeriCache’s, while SparseSpec drops from 1.82×1.82\times to 1.02×1.02\times since it must keep full KV resident on the drafting GPU. Right: as the HBM-to-interconnect ratio falls from 6060 (H100 NVL) to 1010 (GH200), VeriCache’s speedup rises from 1.92×1.92\times to 3.01×3.01\times, as a faster interconnect makes each full-KV reload cheap, so verification fires more often without stalling drafting.

Varying hardware (Pipeline 2).

Figure 13 (Left) sweeps the number of remote gpus divided by the number of local gpus (GR/GLG_{R}/G_{L}), which sets whether the local and remote pools produce and consume speculated tokens at matching rates. Below the sweet spot at GR/GL=4G_{R}/G_{L}{=}4, the remote pool under-supplies drafts and spare local cycles fall back to Full KV; above it, local HBM cannot verify drafts fast enough and spare remote cycles fall back instead—in both regimes the speedup converges back toward 1×1\times. Figure 13 (Right) sweeps Tinit​_​remote/TdecodeT_{\mathrm{init\_remote}}/T_{\mathrm{decode}}, the ratio of remote-KV arrival time to one draft-plus-verify round. Up to 55, streaming a quantized KV over the slow remote network pays off since initial loading dominates the request lifecycle; beyond that, TdecodeT_{\mathrm{decode}} dominates and the benefit fades back toward 1×1\times.

8.3. Comparing with lossy KV

For each lossy baseline we sweep its compression knob to trace the quality–throughput frontier: offline token-dropping methods at compression ratios 0.250.25, 0.50.5, and 0.750.75; online token-dropping methods at KV-cache budgets of 10241024, 20482048, and 40964096 tokens; and quantization methods at 88, 44, and 22 bits.

Quality and throughput on two pipelines.

Figure 14 reports KL-divergence from Full KV vs. decoding throughput across Pipeline 1 (top), Pipeline 2 (bottom), and three models. VeriCache’s KL stays under 0.010.01 nats (attributable to hardware nondeterminism (He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025)) while reaching up to 3.82×3.82\times Full KV’s throughput (Llama-70B, Pipeline 1). The lossy baselines (KVzip, KIVI) must trade quality for throughput: on Llama-70B/Pipeline 1 at compression 0.50.5, KVzip accumulates ∼14.4{\sim}14.4 nats of KL per request—the lossy model emits Full KV’s exact output with probability only e−14.4≈5×10−7e^{-14.4}{\approx}5{\times}10^{-7}. At the highest compression this widens by another ∼12×{\sim}12\times.

Varying datasets.

The same picture holds across task-specific quality metrics on both Pipeline 1 workloads. Figure 16 reports function-call accuracy on ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025): VeriCache reaches at least 59%59\% of the fastest KVzip configuration’s throughput at Full KV accuracy, while KVzip loses up to ∼30{\sim}30 points at the same throughput and collapses to ∼31%{\sim}31\% of Full KV’s accuracy on Llama-70B even at the most conservative ratio. Figure 17 runs long-generation on Qwen-32B with LongGenBench (Wu et al., 2024) (completion rate) and GSM8K-Long (Liu et al., 2024a) (accuracy): VeriCache preserves Full KV’s 100%100\% completion at 339339 tok/s and 90%90\% accuracy at 385385 tok/s. KVzip’s quality drops by around 10 points at the same speed.

Varying compression methods.

Figure 15 adds two token-dropping baselines (ExpectedAttention (Devoto et al., 2025), SnapKV (Li et al., 2024a)) and two quantization baselines (KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024), RotateKV (Su et al., 2025)) on Mistral-24B. Across all four, VeriCache’s KL stays within 0.010.01 nats while running 1.41.4–1.9×1.9\times faster than Full KV; the baselines trace the same quality–throughput frontier as the KVzip/KIVI headlines, accumulating tens of nats of KL.

9. Related Work

KV cache compression.

Token-dropping methods (KVzip (Kim et al., 2025), KVzap (Jegou and Jeblick, 2026)) and quantization (KIVI (Liu et al., 2024c), KVQuant (Hooper et al., 2024)) shrink the KV cache but are inherently lossy (§3). VeriCache turns them lossless by drafting with the compressed cache and verifying against the full one.

Speculative decoding.

Speculative decoding accelerates a target model with a cheaper proposer (EAGLE (Li et al., 2025c; Li et al., 2024b), MTP (Cai et al., 2025), n-gram (Chen et al., 2025a)); these compose with VeriCache. Closer to us, MagicDec (Sadhukhan et al., 2024), QuantSpec (Tiwari et al., 2025), and SparseSpec (Zhao et al., 2025) draft from a sparse/compressed cache but pin the full KV in HBM, ignore remote prefix caching, and hard-wire one compressor—VeriCache addresses all three.

Prefill–decode disaggregation.

Serving systems disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools (DistServe (Zhong et al., 2024), Splitwise (Patel et al., 2024), TetriInfer (Hu et al., 2024), Mooncake (Qin et al., 2024)). Decode nodes hit exactly the HBM-bandwidth bottleneck VeriCache targets, so VeriCache slots directly into a decode pool.

10. Limitations & Future Work

Memory overhead.

VeriCache keeps the full KV cache on CPU (or storage) in addition to the compressed cache on GPU, so it incurs more storage overhead.

Static draft length.

VeriCache uses a fixed draft length per workload; a per-request adaptive policy driven by early accept/reject outcomes would handle heterogeneous compressors and contexts more gracefully.

Drafter-specific compression.

Existing compressors optimize direct-serving accuracy; a compressor designed to maximize acceptance length at large draft horizons—a different objective—could push VeriCache’s throughput further.

Verification beyond compression.

Other lossy KV techniques besides compression—for instance, reusing precomputed KV across non-prefix chunks (CacheBlend (Yao et al., 2025))—also produce outputs that diverge from full-KV decoding. Whether a draft-then-verify approach could help here would be an interesting question to explore.

11. Conclusion

Lossy KV compression speeds up long-context LLM serving while lowering output quality. VeriCache restores lossless inference by drafting from the compressed cache and verifying against the full cache, with cross-resource staggering and long acceptance runs hiding the verification cost. It delivers up to 4×4\times higher throughput than full-KV decoding while producing identical outputs, across both token-dropping and quantization methods.

Appendix A Proof of the KL Chain Rule for Autoregressive Distributions

We prove Eq. (2) from Section 3: for autoregressive distributions pfullp_{\text{full}} and plossyp_{\text{lossy}} over a sequence x1:Tx_{1:T}, the sequence-level KL divergence decomposes additively as

KL(pfull(x1:T)∥plossy(x1:T))=∑t=1T𝔼x<t∼pfull[KLt],\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\text{full}}(x_{1:T})\,\|\,p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{1:T})\right)\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{x_{<t}\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\left[\mathrm{KL}_{t}\right],

where KLt≜KL(pfull(⋅∣x<t)∥plossy(⋅∣x<t))\mathrm{KL}_{t}\;\triangleq\;\mathrm{KL}\!\left(p_{\text{full}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\,\|\,p_{\text{lossy}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})\right) is the per-step KL at decoding step tt given the prefix x<tx_{<t}.

Proof.

For brevity, let

ℓt​(x≤t)≜log⁡pfull​(xt∣x<t)plossy​(xt∣x<t)\ell_{t}(x_{\leq t})\;\triangleq\;\log\frac{p_{\text{full}}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})}{p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{t}\mid x_{<t})}

denote the per-step log-likelihood ratio. By the chain rule of probability, both joint distributions factor as p(x1:T)=∏t=1Tp(xt∣x<t)p(x_{1:T})=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(x_{t}\mid x_{<t}), so

logpfull(x1:T)plossy(x1:T)=∑t=1Tℓt(x≤t).\log\frac{p_{\text{full}}(x_{1:T})}{p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{1:T})}\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(x_{\leq t}).

By definition, the sequence-level KL is the expected log-likelihood ratio under pfullp_{\text{full}}:

KL1:T\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}_{1:T} =𝔼x1:T∼pfull[logpfull(x1:T)plossy(x1:T)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x_{1:T}\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\left[\log\tfrac{p_{\text{full}}(x_{1:T})}{p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{1:T})}\right]
=∑t=1T𝔼x1:T∼pfull[ℓt(x≤t)].\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{x_{1:T}\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\left[\ell_{t}(x_{\leq t})\right].

Each ℓt\ell_{t} depends only on x≤tx_{\leq t}, so by the tower property,

𝔼x1:T∼pfull[ℓt(x≤t)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x_{1:T}\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\left[\ell_{t}(x_{\leq t})\right] =𝔼x<t∼pfull[𝔼xt∼pfull(⋅∣x<t)[ℓt(x≤t)]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x_{<t}\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\left[\mathbb{E}_{x_{t}\sim p_{\text{full}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})}\!\left[\ell_{t}(x_{\leq t})\right]\right]
=𝔼x<t∼pfull​[KLt],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x_{<t}\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\left[\mathrm{KL}_{t}\right],

where the last equality uses the fact that the inner expectation, 𝔼xt∼pfull(⋅∣x<t)[ℓt]\mathbb{E}_{x_{t}\sim p_{\text{full}}(\cdot\mid x_{<t})}[\ell_{t}], is exactly the per-step KL conditioned on x<tx_{<t}. Substituting back,

KL1:T=∑t=1T𝔼x<t∼pfull[KLt].■\mathrm{KL}_{1:T}\;=\;\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{x_{<t}\sim p_{\text{full}}}\!\left[\mathrm{KL}_{t}\right].\qquad\blacksquare
Implication.

If the per-step KL is bounded below by some ε>0\varepsilon>0 on average—i.e., 𝔼x<t∼pfull​[KLt]≥ε\mathbb{E}_{x_{<t}\sim p_{\text{full}}}[\mathrm{KL}_{t}]\geq\varepsilon for all tt—then KL1:T≥εT\mathrm{KL}_{1:T}\geq\varepsilon T grows at least linearly in the output length TT. Because KL1:T=𝔼x∼pfull[log(pfull(x1:T)/plossy(x1:T))]\mathrm{KL}_{1:T}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\text{full}}}[\log(p_{\text{full}}(x_{1:T})/p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{1:T}))], this means the expected log-likelihood ratio under pfullp_{\text{full}} grows linearly in TT. Equivalently, for a sample x1:T∼pfullx_{1:T}\sim p_{\text{full}}, the log-likelihood ratio log(pfull(x1:T)/plossy(x1:T))\log(p_{\text{full}}(x_{1:T})/p_{\text{lossy}}(x_{1:T})) has mean ≥ε​T{\geq}\,\varepsilon T, so the likelihood ratio itself is typically of order eε​Te^{\varepsilon T}—i.e., exponential in TT.

Appendix B Full Theoretical Analysis

This appendix provides the complete derivations for the throughput models summarized in Section 4.

B.1. Intra-request KV access

We consider a single GPU serving BB homogeneous long-context decoding requests in steady state, where each request has the same context length and thus the same KV cache size KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{full}}. We focus on the decode phase, which is HBM-bandwidth-bound for long-context workloads. Table 3 summarizes the notation used throughout this analysis. All requests speculate: each cycles through xx draft iterations (using compressed KV) followed by one verification iteration (using full KV). A request is either non-offloaded (BgB_{g}: full KV remains on GPU) or offloaded (BcB_{c}: full KV resides on CPU). Non-offloaded requests verify for free since the full KV is already on GPU; offloaded requests must reload the full KV from CPU for verification. In steady state, xx+1​Bc\frac{x}{x+1}B_{c} offloaded requests are drafting and 1x+1​Bc\frac{1}{x+1}B_{c} are verifying, giving an average GPU KV footprint per offloaded request of:

(5) KVavg=KVfull⋅x​c+1x+1.\text{KV}_{\text{avg}}=\text{KV}_{\text{full}}\cdot\frac{xc+1}{x+1}.

GPU memory constraint. Since KVavg<KVfull\text{KV}_{\text{avg}}<\text{KV}_{\text{full}}, VeriCache serves a larger batch than the baseline:

(6) M+Bg⋅KVfull+Bc⋅KVavg≤GPUmem.M+B_{g}\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}+B_{c}\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{avg}}\leq\text{GPU}_{\text{mem}}.

Per-iteration time. The GPU time is bounded by HBM bandwidth:

(7) Tgpu=M+B⋅KVavgBWhbm.T_{\text{gpu}}=\frac{M+B\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{avg}}}{\text{BW}_{\text{hbm}}}.

Each offloaded verification requires transferring the extra KV of size (1−c)⋅KVfull(1{-}c)\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}} from CPU to GPU. Rather than assuming each reload completes within a single iteration, we let ℓ\ell denote the number of iterations a single reload spans (cycles per load). Spreading the transfer over ℓ\ell iterations reduces the per-iteration interconnect demand:

(8) Txfer=Bc⋅(1−c)⋅KVfull(x+1)⋅BWinter⋅ℓ.T_{\text{xfer}}=\frac{B_{c}\cdot(1-c)\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}}{(x+1)\cdot\text{BW}_{\text{inter}}\cdot\ell}.

However, the interconnect can only sustain one in-flight reload at a time, which constrains the arrival rate of new loads:

(9) Bcx+1⋅ℓ≤1.\frac{B_{c}}{x+1}\cdot\ell\leq 1.

Since HBM reads and interconnect transfers use distinct hardware, they overlap:

(10) Titer=max⁡(Tgpu,Txfer).T_{\text{iter}}=\max(T_{\text{gpu}},\;T_{\text{xfer}}).

Throughput. All requests produce γ⁡(x,c)⋅x+1x+1\frac{\gamma(x,c)\cdot x+1}{x+1} tokens per iteration on average, where γ⁡(x,c)\gamma(x,c) is the acceptance rate as a function of draft length and compression ratio. The scheduler chooses BcB_{c}, xx, cc, and ℓ\ell to maximize throughput:

maxBc,x,c,ℓ\displaystyle\max_{B_{c},\,x,\,c,\,\ell}\;\; B⋅γ⁡(x,c)⋅x+1x+1max⁡(Tgpu,Txfer)\displaystyle\frac{B\cdot\frac{\gamma(x,c)\cdot x+1}{x+1}}{\max\!\left(T_{\text{gpu}},\;\;T_{\text{xfer}}\right)}
s.t.   Eqs. (6), (9),​ 0≤Bc≤B,\displaystyle\text{Eqs.~(\ref{eq:mem_constraint_app}),~(\ref{eq:load_constraint_app}),}\;0\leq B_{c}\leq B,
(11) x≥1, 0<c<1,ℓ≥1.\displaystyle x\geq 1,\;0<c<1,\;\ell\geq 1.

The four knobs navigate a trade-off between TgpuT_{\text{gpu}}, TxferT_{\text{xfer}}, and the effective tokens per iteration. Increasing BcB_{c} lowers TgpuT_{\text{gpu}} (smaller per-request HBM footprint enables larger batches and faster reads) but raises TxferT_{\text{xfer}} (more offloaded requests require more interconnect transfers). Increasing ℓ\ell reduces TxferT_{\text{xfer}} by spreading each reload over more iterations, but the constraint Bcx+1⋅ℓ≤1\frac{B_{c}}{x+1}\cdot\ell\leq 1 forces either fewer offloaded requests or longer draft sequences. Decreasing cc further reduces TgpuT_{\text{gpu}} by shrinking the compressed KV size, but also lowers γ⁡(x,c)\gamma(x,c), reducing the number of accepted tokens per iteration. Increasing xx amortizes the interconnect cost over more draft tokens (lowering TxferT_{\text{xfer}}), but γ⁡(x,c)\gamma(x,c) decreases with longer drafts, yielding diminishing returns in accepted tokens.

The full KV baseline (Bc=0B_{c}{=}0) serves at most ⌊(GPUmem−M)/KVfull⌋\lfloor(\text{GPU}_{\text{mem}}{-}M)/\text{KV}_{\text{full}}\rfloor requests; pure lossy decoding serves up to 1/c×1/c\times more but sacrifices exactness. VeriCache operates between these extremes while maintaining lossless output.

B.2. Inter-request KV reuse

We consider a cluster with GLG_{L} local GPUs close to a KV storage node (bandwidth BWh\text{BW}_{h}) and GRG_{R} remote GPUs connected via a slower link (bandwidth BWl\text{BW}_{l}, with BWh≫BWl\text{BW}_{h}\gg\text{BW}_{l}). Each request reuses a pre-computed KV cache from storage and must generate KK output tokens. Here, for simplicity, we assume all requests have the same KV size and output length. We consider KV quantization methods where the KV cache is compressed offline to reduce network transfer size (c⋅KVfullc\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}} bytes) but is decompressed to full size on the GPU upon reuse.

Derived quantities. Each GPU can batch at most Bmax=⌊(GPUmem−M)/KVfull⌋B_{\text{max}}=\lfloor(\text{GPU}_{\text{mem}}{-}M)/\text{KV}_{\text{full}}\rfloor requests. The per-request per-token decode time depends on the actual batch occupancy BB of that GPU:

(12) Ttok​(B)=M/B+KVfullBWhbm.T_{\text{tok}}(B)=\frac{M/B+\text{KV}_{\text{full}}}{\text{BW}_{\text{hbm}}}.

Since model weights MM are shared across the batch, TtokT_{\text{tok}} decreases as BB grows and reaches its minimum at B=BmaxB=B_{\text{max}}. Network transfer times per request are Th=KVfull/BWhT_{h}=\text{KV}_{\text{full}}/\text{BW}_{h} (full KV to local), Tl=KVfull/BWlT_{l}=\text{KV}_{\text{full}}/\text{BW}_{l} (full KV to remote), Tlc=c⋅KVfull/BWlT_{l}^{c}=c\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}/\text{BW}_{l} (compressed KV to remote), and Tlrem=(1−c)⋅KVfull/BWlT_{l}^{\text{rem}}=(1{-}c)\cdot\text{KV}_{\text{full}}/\text{BW}_{l} (remaining KV to remote).

Resource model. We model each GPU pool with three resources: network time (how long the per-GPU network link is active), GPU compute time (how long the GPU computes), and memory-time (how long a memory slot is occupied). Although network and compute are serialized within a single request, they use distinct hardware and can be pipelined across requests: one request’s KV transfer overlaps with another request’s decode on the same GPU. The capacity constraints are:

(13) ∑iLinet⋅ni\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i}L_{i}^{\text{net}}\cdot n_{i} ≤GL,\displaystyle\leq G_{L},
(14) ∑iLigpu⋅ni\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i}L_{i}^{\text{gpu}}\cdot n_{i} ≤GL,\displaystyle\leq G_{L},
(15) ∑iLimem⋅ni\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i}L_{i}^{\text{mem}}\cdot n_{i} ≤GL⋅Bmax,\displaystyle\leq G_{L}\cdot B_{\text{max}},
(16) ∑iRinet⋅ni\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i}R_{i}^{\text{net}}\cdot n_{i} ≤GR,\displaystyle\leq G_{R},
(17) ∑iRigpu⋅ni\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i}R_{i}^{\text{gpu}}\cdot n_{i} ≤GR,\displaystyle\leq G_{R},
(18) ∑iRimem⋅ni\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i}R_{i}^{\text{mem}}\cdot n_{i} ≤GR⋅Bmax,\displaystyle\leq G_{R}\cdot B_{\text{max}},

where nin_{i} is the throughput (requests per second) assigned to path ii, and LinetL_{i}^{\text{net}}, LigpuL_{i}^{\text{gpu}}, LimemL_{i}^{\text{mem}}, RinetR_{i}^{\text{net}}, RigpuR_{i}^{\text{gpu}}, RimemR_{i}^{\text{mem}} are the per-request local and remote costs (in seconds). Memory-time equals the wall-clock duration a slot is occupied (transfer plus compute), and may exceed GPU compute time when KV is cached between verification rounds.

Baseline paths. Two paths are available without VeriCache:

  • •

    B1 (pure local): Transfer full KV to local, decode KK tokens. Lnet=ThL^{\text{net}}{=}T_{h}, Lgpu=K⋅TtokL^{\text{gpu}}{=}K\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, Lmem=Th+K⋅TtokL^{\text{mem}}{=}T_{h}+K\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, R=0R{=}0.

  • •

    B2 (pure remote): Transfer full KV to remote, decode KK tokens. Rnet=TlR^{\text{net}}{=}T_{l}, Rgpu=K⋅TtokR^{\text{gpu}}{=}K\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, Rmem=Tl+K⋅TtokR^{\text{mem}}{=}T_{l}+K\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, L=0L{=}0.

VeriCache paths. VeriCache adds two speculative paths that exploit the gap between compressed and full transfer times.

P1 (verify-only, no full KV to remote). Remote receives compressed KV (TlcT_{l}^{c}) and drafts K/γK/\gamma tokens with lossy KV. Local receives full KV (ThT_{h}) and verifies in N1=⌈K/(γ​x)⌉N_{1}=\lceil K/(\gamma x)\rceil rounds of xx draft tokens each. Since local GPU memory is limited, KV may be evicted between rounds. We model two variants:

  • •

    Cached: KV stays on local GPU across rounds. Lnet=ThL^{\text{net}}=T_{h}, Lgpu=N1⋅TtokL^{\text{gpu}}=N_{1}\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, Lmem=Th+(K/γ)⋅TtokL^{\text{mem}}=T_{h}+(K/\gamma)\cdot T_{\text{tok}} (slot held during entire draft phase).

  • •

    Stateless: KV re-transferred each round. Lnet=N1⋅ThL^{\text{net}}=N_{1}\cdot T_{h}, Lgpu=N1⋅TtokL^{\text{gpu}}=N_{1}\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, Lmem=N1⋅(Th+Ttok)L^{\text{mem}}=N_{1}\cdot(T_{h}+T_{\text{tok}}).

In both cases, Rnet=TlcR^{\text{net}}=T_{l}^{c}, Rgpu=(K/γ)⋅TtokR^{\text{gpu}}=(K/\gamma)\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, Rmem=Tlc+(K/γ)⋅TtokR^{\text{mem}}=T_{l}^{c}+(K/\gamma)\cdot T_{\text{tok}}. P1 is efficient for short outputs where streaming full KV to remote is wasteful.

P2 (stream full KV to remote + AR). Remote receives compressed KV (TlcT_{l}^{c}) and begins drafting immediately. In parallel, the remaining KV streams to remote (TlremT_{l}^{\text{rem}}). During this streaming window, remote produces Ndraft=min⁡(Tlrem/Ttok,K/γ)N_{\text{draft}}=\min(T_{l}^{\text{rem}}/T_{\text{tok}},\;K/\gamma) draft tokens, verified by local in N2=⌈Ndraft/x⌉N_{2}=\lceil N_{\text{draft}}/x\rceil rounds. Once the full KV arrives, remote completes the remaining K2=max⁡(0,K−γ⋅Ndraft)K_{2}=\max(0,\;K-\gamma\cdot N_{\text{draft}}) tokens via standard decode.

  • •

    Remote: Rnet=Tlc+TlremR^{\text{net}}=T_{l}^{c}+T_{l}^{\text{rem}}, Rgpu=(Ndraft+K2)⋅TtokR^{\text{gpu}}=(N_{\text{draft}}+K_{2})\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, Rmem=Tlc+max⁡(Ndraft⋅Ttok,Tlrem)+K2⋅TtokR^{\text{mem}}=T_{l}^{c}+\max(N_{\text{draft}}\cdot T_{\text{tok}},\;T_{l}^{\text{rem}})+K_{2}\cdot T_{\text{tok}}.

  • •

    Local cached: Lnet=ThL^{\text{net}}=T_{h}, Lgpu=N2⋅TtokL^{\text{gpu}}=N_{2}\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, Lmem=Th+Ndraft⋅TtokL^{\text{mem}}=T_{h}+N_{\text{draft}}\cdot T_{\text{tok}}.

  • •

    Local stateless: Lnet=N2⋅ThL^{\text{net}}=N_{2}\cdot T_{h}, Lgpu=N2⋅TtokL^{\text{gpu}}=N_{2}\cdot T_{\text{tok}}, Lmem=N2⋅(Th+Ttok)L^{\text{mem}}=N_{2}\cdot(T_{h}+T_{\text{tok}}).

P2 is efficient for long outputs where the streaming window amortizes the cost of transferring full KV.

Throughput optimization. With all six paths {B1, B2, P1-cached, P1-stateless, P2-cached, P2-stateless}, the system maximizes total throughput (in tok/s):

(19) max{ni≥0}K⋅∑inis.t. Eqs. (13)\max_{\{n_{i}\geq 0\}}\;\;K\cdot\textstyle\sum_{i}n_{i}\quad\text{s.t. Eqs.~(\ref{eq:cap_app})}

where the resource costs in Eqs. (13) are evaluated at the actual batch occupancies implied by {ni}\{n_{i}\}. The optimizer naturally selects the best mix: P1 for short outputs, P2 for long outputs, cached verification when local memory is abundant, stateless when local compute is abundant, and baseline paths when speculation offers no benefit.

Appendix C Ideal Speedup Calculation for Speculative-Decoding Comparisons

This calculation extends the intra-request throughput model of Appendix B.1 to a two-level speculation scheme. VeriCache proposes xx outer tokens using the target model on compressed KV (the same xx and γ⁡(x,c)\gamma(x,c) as Appendix B.1); an auxiliary drafter (Eagle, MTP-head) proposes de−1d_{e}-1 additional tokens at each outer position.

Under chain-independence of the two drafters, the expected accepted draft length per cycle becomes

γ⁡(x,c)⋅x⋅[ 1+γe​(de)⋅(de−1)],\gamma(x,c)\cdot x\cdot\big[\,1+\gamma_{e}(d_{e})\cdot(d_{e}-1)\,\big],

i.e., VeriCache’s accepted length γ⁡(x,c)⋅x\gamma(x,c)\cdot x from Eq. (11) scaled by the composition multiplier [1+γe​(de)​(de−1)][1+\gamma_{e}(d_{e})(d_{e}-1)].
